rows.title: Ethics and Moral Reasoning in Criminal Justice
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify ethical issues that often arise for criminal justice professionals.
Analyze theories of moral development and leadership and their influence on ethical problem solving.
Compare common theories of ethical decision making and methods to reinforce procedural practices and social justice in a diverse society.
Apply ethical principles and standards of justice to cases involving police corruption, abuse of power, and judicial/attorney misconduct.

rows.title: Principles and Procedures of the Justice System
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and describe the stages in the trial process
Identify and critically analyze the concepts of due process as found in the 6th, 8th, and 14th amendments, including right to counsel, bail, and jury trial
Describe the history and application of the exclusionary rule in shaping criminal procedure
Describe application of the right to counsel in a criminal case
Describe application of the right to a jury trial

rows.title: Criminal Investigation
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Execute appropriate preliminary investigation related to crime scene examination.
Analyze various investigative techniques for specific criminal offenses.
Distinguish critical ethical issues.
Analyze the investigator's role that leads to criminal court proceedings and the trial process.

rows.title: Forensic Evidence
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Summarize the history of forensic science, the structure and organization of crime labs, and the sub-disciplines of forensic science.
Explain the roles of forensic and investigative personnel and articulate a realistic perspective of the field of forensic science.
Select the appropriate methods of analysis used for biological, chemical, physical fit, and pattern evidence.
Evaluate the criteria for admission of scientific evidence in court and expert testimony, and the types and sources of error in forensic science.

rows.title: Patrol Procedures
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the basic functions and purpose of police patrol.
Describe police procedures and codes of conduct.
Demonstrate required skills for San Francisco City College Campus Police Department patrol.
Describe the knowledge and physical skills necessary in preparing for the San Francisco Police Department entrance examination.

rows.title: Criminal Justice Work Experience
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Utilize a glossary of terms and definitions unique to the assigned agency
Describe the functions and services provided by the assigned agency in order to complete assigned tasks
Illustrate professional attitudes while working with the public and members at the internship site
Display promptness, responsibility and courtesy in the work experience agency
Compare the theoretical and practical functions of the criminal justice system relative to the agency assigned

rows.title: The Black Experience in California
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate the scholarly work of African Americans to explain the historical and political reasons Africans were brought to the "New World" during the Early Colonial Era and the ensuing social struggles and lived experiences of African American communities.

Analyze how race and racism impacted the cultural realities and experiences of early African and African American people in California in areas such as class, gender, language, national origin, religion, sexuality, sovereignty, and spirituality.
Utilize historical sources to analyze how the intersectionality of race and racism has shaped survival techniques and cultural identity of African Americans in California.
Analyze effective interpersonal and inter-ethnic group interactions for African people to successfully gain agency and thrive in the American West and the U.S.

rows.title: American Sign Language Part I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and use American Sign Language with elementary linguistic structures appropriate to a variety of language functions.
Explain general historical factors and contexts that have contributed to American Deaf culture and the development of American Sign Language.
Examine culturally appropriate behavior with Deaf people in various social situations.

rows.title: Indigenous Peoples of North America
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the relationship of North American indigenous cultures and the natural environment using the anthropological culture area approach.
Compare different traditional North American indigenous cultures in a nonethnocentric manner using anthropological concepts.
Analyze and contrast anthropological and non-anthropological sources of information about indigenous North American cultures.
Analyze precontact and postcontact North American indigenous cultures using an anthropological perspective.
Compare traditional North American indigenous cultures with present day North American indigenous cultures.
Analyze challenges faced by Native American indigenous peoples today in relationship to sociopolitical and economic issues.

rows.title: Queer Anthropology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and apply key terminology and methods in the study of queer anthropology.
Compare key theoretical frameworks that influence the perceptions and experiences of queer individuals around the world.
Analyze the major institutions, cultural forces, and practices that determine queer status.
Assess how anthropology contributes to our understanding of global conceptions of queer cultures.

rows.title: Introduction to Linguistic Anthropology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the nature and structure of human language, and compare its acquisition process to various forms of non-verbal communication.
Use the methods of phonological analysis to assess individual languages.
Describe the biological foundations of language, and the relationships between language and thought.
Examine the influence of language on values, behavior, and inter- and intra-cultural exchanges.
Describe linguistic change and the lexical reconstruction method used to infer time span, movements, and overall cultural content of population groups.

rows.title: Architecture Design Studio I
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Create architectonic solutions to a set of abstract problems
Evaluate a proposed architectonic solution against the problem requirements
Analyze and communicate designs and design precedents visually, orally, and in physical model using an architectural vocabulary
Apply a visual language that is two- and three-dimensional responsive to form, space, and context
Examine how architects and interior designers create sets of functional and sustainable solutions

rows.title: Fundamentals of Building Structures
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Consider the major constraints and impacts related to the selection of structural systems
Explain how structural systems respond to loads, including natural forces
Assess the performance of materials in a structural system

rows.title: Fundamentals of Rhino 3D
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Navigate the software's interface, work flow, and NURBS geometry.
Create three-dimensional digital models using 3D basic modeling tools, poly-surfaces and modeling aids to represent a designed object.
Modify, edit, analyze, and transform existing digital three-dimensional surface models, using algorithms to create and edit 3D geometry.
Construct a prototype, document with annotation, and render a digital three-dimensional surface model.

rows.title: Freehand Drawing II
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply freehand drawing skills (without the use of straight edge tools) to create sketches of the existing or proposed built environment using correct proportions.
Recall the key components of linear perspective and analyze their principles in communicating form in the built environment.
Employ one-point, two-point and three-point linear perspective techniques in freehand drawing to analyze architectural form, structure and context.
Use varied monochromatic and polychromatic drawing media to depict form, value and texture in freehand drawing.

rows.title: Ancient Art and Architecture of Latin America
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the different art styles of the major cultures of ancient Latin America.
Compare selected ancient Latin American cultures and their beliefs.
Analyze how Latin American ancient art styles reflect their cultural context.
Analyze how geographical locations and conditions are reflected in the beliefs, styles, and customs of each culture.

rows.title: History of Contemporary Art
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the variety of techniques and formal visual elements of individual works of art in different media.
Define the various styles of late modern and contemporary art to analyze their components and characteristics.
Evaluate the historical factors which led to the emergence, development and subsequent history of late modern and contemporary art movements/styles.
Examine and assess works of art in relation to the historical, cultural, and sociological context in which they were created.
Compare stylistic elements that distinguish aesthetic and cultural trends of pivotal works of art by major artists in late modern and contemporary art.

rows.title: 18th-Century French Art
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and differentiate 18th-century works of French art with reference to formal elements and style.
Identify connections between 18th-century French art and ideas.
Analyze the social functions of art in 18th-century France.
Evaluate the historical significance of 18th-century French art.

rows.title: Advanced Design: 3D Foundations
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Create three-dimensional forms that demonstrate basic knowledge and understanding of elements and organizing principles of design.
Employ innovative problem solving through the use of materials and development of form when designing for a specific problem.
Apply careful and thoughtful elementary visual analysis of three-dimensional form through writing and verbal discussion.
Identify the use of design principles and elements in the creation of design and art objects in various cultures throughout history.

rows.title: Beginning Figure Drawing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply beginning-level drawing techniques and media to accurately draw proportional human figures from life.
Apply a beginning-level understanding of major muscle groups and bone structures to figure drawing.
Analyze figure drawings across diverse cultural contexts, exploring beginning-level formal qualities and social-historical significance.
Analyze one's own work and the work of peers using beginning-level critical thinking skills and vocabulary.

rows.title: Beginning Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Employ materials and techniques fundamental to the construction of paintings in several styles and genres.
Organize elements of design and color into effective painted compositions.
Apply the skills necessary to develop ideas into personally-expressive paintings.
Analyze historical and contemporary styles of painting and discuss their relevance to painting now.

rows.title: Intermediate Chinese Brush Painting
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply intermediate-level techniques in classical and contemporary Chinese calligraphy and painting using traditional materials.
Analyze the poetic, philosophical, and symbolic content in historical and contemporary Chinese brush paintings to inform expressive personal work.
Utilize traditional Chinese aesthetic principles—such as the use of color, line, shape, layering, and tonal variation—to solve visual problems at the intermediate level.
Evaluate student's own brush paintings and those of peers in terms of formal qualities, technical execution, cultural content, and expressive intent.

rows.title: Intermediate Ceramics
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply new skills and techniques to create artwork at the intermediate level.
Integrate three-dimensional design principles as they apply to structure and aesthetics in artwork at an intermediate level.
Evaluate artwork in a critical thinking process that supports individual creative expression at an intermediate level.
Research contemporary and historical ceramics that relate to the students’ personal artwork.

rows.title: Survey of Art from Prehistory to the Medieval Era
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from prehistory to the medieval era employing appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze works of art and architecture in terms of aesthetic, socio-political, religious, historical, technological, and cultural contexts in which they were created.
Develop critical thinking, information literacy, and problem solving through an engagement with art, architecture, artists, and patrons from prehistory to the medieval era.

rows.title: Asian American Experience Since 1820
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the impact of racialized and ethnocentric United States government policies on Asian immigrants and Asian American participation in civic duties and social justice movements.
Apply Asian American produced theories and methodologies of social and behavioral science inquiry in Asian American Studies.
Analyze intersectionality within the Asian American experience in the United States, as race and racism relate to age, class, gender, language, national origin, religion, and sexuality.

Summarize the diverse Asian immigration experience, including socio-cultural, economic and political conditions, critical events, histories and traditions, that have impacted Asian American communities’ efforts to gain agency and build an equitable and just society.

Review critically how Asian American struggles and resistance for racial and social justice, solidarity, and liberation, as experienced and enacted by diverse communities, are relevant to current and structural issues

rows.title: Asian American Issues Through Film
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze and articulate how society influences the interpretation and message of films, specifically with regard to race and ethnicity, critically reviewing the intertextual relationships between Asian American historical archetypes in American cinema.

Analyze representations by both mainstream and independent media of the intersectionality of race and racism with class, gender, sexuality, religion, immigration status and other aspects of Asian American lived experiences and their impact on Asian Americans.

Assess the critical impacts of independent productions in Asian American media on American mainstream representations of Asian Americans, interpreting those portrayals in relation to struggle, social justice, current issues and national policies.

Evaluate the ways diasporic or transnational cinema from Asia influence representations of Asian Americans in American media, including applying Ethnic Studies theory and knowledge to describe the connection between film portrayals and critical events in the histories, cultures and intellectual traditions, with special focus on agency and group-affirmation.

Compare similar film content from different perspectives (outsider perspectives versus insider perspectives), applying theories and methodologies of social and behavioral science and Ethnic Studies in the exploration of Asian American films.

Formulate an analytical Ethnic Studies framework for uncovering, evaluating, and challenging stereotypes, bias, and misrepresentation in films, by articulating Ethnic Studies concepts such as race and racism, racialization, and anti-racism in analyzing film images of Asians.

rows.title: Stories of Asian America
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate critically the intersection of race and racism with gender, class, sexuality, spirituality, national origin, immigration status, ability, language, and/or age, as expressed in literature and lived experiences of Asian Americans.

Analyze the critical content and contexts of Asian American writings within the social, historical, intellectual traditions of lived-experiences, emphasizing agency and group-affirmation and applying knowledge and theory produced by Asian American authors.
Evaluate sources of tension and conflict within Asian American families and identity, as represented in literature, particularly along lines of gender and generation.

Assess the contributions Asian American creative expression has made to America, applying an aesthetic understanding of the ways in which Asian Americans have created fine and performing arts, linguistic expression, philosophical reasoning, and analytical or creative writing.

Analyze through literature the impact of migration on community formation and transnational connections, exploring communal, national, international, and transnational structural issues, Asian American resistance and struggles for racial and social justice.
Describe and actively engage with how Asian American authors and communities have approached anti-racist and anti-colonial issues, practices, and movements to build a more just and equitable society.

rows.title: East Asian Calligraphy: An Introduction
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Comprehend writing systems, scripts, and aesthetic principles of East Asian calligraphy in cultural/historical backgrounds.
Analyze the relationship between calligraphy and philosophy/religion/art in China, Japan, and Korea.
Practice the discipline, techniques, and training of East Asian calligraphy.

rows.title: Observational Astronomy
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and locate a broad range of celestial objects
Predict the motions of the sun, moon, and planets from the heliocentric and geocentric viewpoints
Analyze and characterize morphologies and spectra to understand the classification of celestial objects.
Examine systemic challenges with astronomical devices.
Analyze data from various astronomical devices to compare celestial objects' characteristics to established classification systems.

rows.title: Life in the Universe
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assess the role of the stellar evolution process as the mechanism for the creation of the elements necessary for life.
Describe how the orbital and physical characteristics of solar system objects affect their potential for life.
Synthesize evidence that supports life on Earth originated from a common ancestor.

Analyze, and classify the major components and adaptation of microbial cells and how microbes persist, interact, and survive within changing and sometimes extreme environments to understand the origin of life.
Compare the major techniques used and results to date in the search for extra-solar planets and life beyond Earth.

rows.title: Welded Panel Repair and Replacement
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe and observe all auto body shop safety practices related to welded panel repair and replacement.
Evaluate repair costs with detailed attention to estimation of welded panel damage, parts and materials, and labor times.
Describe vehicle structures, types, metal, and materials used in auto body construction.
Describe a variety of fusion welding automotive body panels.
Apply corrosion protection best practices when repairing or replacing a welded vehicle panel.

rows.title: Plastic Repair & Refinishing
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe and employ auto shop safety practices related to plastic repair and refinishing.
Calculate repair costs by writing up and estimating plastic damage repair, convert labor times to dollar costs, and estimate paint and material costs.
Identify and repair auto and truck plastic part damage using plastic welding and adhesive repair methods
Perform the basic refinishing steps in plastic repair and plastic parts painting and refinishing.

rows.title: Automotive Electrical
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assess vehicle electrical system parts, operation, and nomenclature.
Diagnose and repair vehicle electrical faults.
Evaluate root cause of circuit malfunctions for proper repair.

rows.title: Engine Performance and Drivability
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assess vehicle engine control system parts, operation, and nomenclature.
Diagnose and repair vehicle fuel injection components.
Evaluate and repair vehicle fuel injection systems.

rows.title: Automotive Braking Systems
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Assess brake system parts, operation, and nomenclature.
Diagnose and repair brake hydraulic systems.
Evaluate and repair power brake and anti-lock brake systems.

rows.title: Media Literacy
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Interpret the meanings of specific forms of media using common methods of media criticism.
Evaluate media representations of social groups and social institutions for their ideological themes.
Apply media literacy concepts and skills to the planning of ethical media messages.
Integrate social and behavioral theory and research into the analysis of the audience's role in media literacy.
Assess the quality of information presented in truth-based media through verification and fact-checking methods.

rows.title: Digital Media Skills
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply basic knowledge of software and hardware commonly used in audio/video/multimedia production.
Move and edit media projects across platforms and between different software programs and convert to various formats.
Use foundational audio/video/multimedia production techniques as applied to creative media projects.
Explain issues and impacts of new technology in the broadcast industries.

rows.title: Music Recording Studio
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe and apply the basic principles of the stages of multi-track audio production.
Operate common professional studio recording equipment.
Apply appropriate microphone placement, gain structure, and signal flow for a multiple source recording session.
Display professionalism and knowledge of workforce protocol in communication and behavior in the recording studio.

rows.title: Sound Reinforcement
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate and use audio equipment required for public address, recording, and broadcast of a live sound event production.
Describe and analyze the technology and skills required to engineer a live sound event from the front-of-house (FOH), monitor, and systems engineer roles.
Troubleshoot a technical failure in the equipment chain of a live sound system and demonstrate methods to remedy the failure.
Display professional communication and collaboration skills as a sound reinforcement team member.

rows.title: Field Video Production
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Set up, operate, and break down video field production equipment.
Create effective and meaningful video programs by applying aesthetic theories from class.
Produce video programs by applying the production phases, including pre-production planning.
Communicate and collaborate effectively as a video production team member, using proper production terminology.

rows.title: Edit & Color DaVinci Resolve
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze media to complete short to mid-length digital video editing projects using visual storytelling and technical approaches common to the industry.
Evaluate and integrate a variety of storytelling and/or genre-related editing techniques at an intermediate level.
Apply concepts of exposure, contrast, and color to improve or enhance video clips, sequences and projects.
Apply appropriate audio correction, visual effects, and graphic elements at an intermediate level.

rows.title: College Internship
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Perform essential tasks appropriate for the college media workplace environment
Formulate reasonable and measurable occupational learning objectives
Analyze work experiences and their relevance to one's educational and/or occupational goals

rows.title: General Biology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe how the theory of evolution explains the unity and diversity of living forms using examples from biochemistry, cell biology, genetics, and organism form and function.
Construct an argument that is based on evidence for how form relates to function in both small scale (molecules and subcellular parts) and large scale (animal physiology) systems.
Evaluate the effects of gene expression and environmental influences on the growth and behavior of organisms.
Synthesize biological information, use quantitative reasoning, and solve critical thinking problems.
Apply the process of science and the skills necessary to successfully and safely carry out laboratory experiments.

rows.title: Science of Living Organisms
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Classify living organisms using phylogenetic and genetic analysis.
Apply the theory of evolution to explain the morphology and adaptive strategies of organisms.
Communicate the interrelationships between organisms using ecological concepts and the impact of human interaction with the natural world.
Apply principles of genetics to genetic engineering methodologies and describe their impact on issues impacting society.
Investigate scientific principles in the laboratory including the analysis and communication of scientific data.

rows.title: Introduction to Entomology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze the biogeographical factors that determine the distribution and impact of arthropod populations.
Compare how various adaptations have contributed to the survivability of arthropods.
Evaluate the importance of arthropod organisms with regard to trophic relationships.
Distinguish differences between the arthropod groups.
Apply scientific principles and the scientific method to critiques of literature and media concerning entomology.

rows.title: Principles of Food Safety
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply biological principles of microbial growth to ensure food safety through each step in the food preparation, service, storage, and transportation processes.
Articulate how a food service environment can meet FDA Food Code recommendations for facilities, equipment, and employee hygiene.
Manipulate environmental conditions in food to support the growth of fermentation microbes in food preparation.

rows.title: Plant Ecology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain the processes that influence species' distribution and abundance using examples of populations and communities shaped by these processes.
Compare and contrast form and function for the major plant phyla and correlate this to the evolution of land plants.
Discuss interactions between species and the environment that determine community composition and structure.
Explain how models and other analytical techniques are used to explain population growth, community structure and ecosystem dynamics.
Observe patterns and generate hypotheses, conduct scientific experiments, and apply critical thinking to explain results.
Apply ecological principles to current conservation issues and critically analyze and explain papers from tbe ecological literature.

rows.title: Ecology of San Francisco Bay
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Apply the process of science and the scientific method, and demonstrate an understanding of the the relationship between scientific research and established knowledge pertaining to ecology.

Illustrate the interdisciplinary nature of ecology by outlining contributions from the natural sciences, social sciences, and engineering and technology to our understanding of human impacts San Francisco Bay.

Analyze and integrate evidence from research in natural science, social science, engineering, and technology to critically evaluate proposed solutions to environmental and resource issues facing San Francisco Bay
Summarize ecological issues of San Francisco Bay, demonstrating content knowledge of key ecological concepts and their social, political, and historical context.
Identify organisms common to San Francisco, explain their adaptations and analyze their role in their community.

rows.title: Ecology of Coastal Mendocino County
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify key drivers and processes that affect the community structure and dynamics of Coastal Mendocino ecosystems.
Understand ecological concepts and apply them to management issues faced within the coastal Mendocino County.

Analyze and integrate evidence from research in natural science, social science, engineering, and technology to critically evaluate proposed solutions to environmental and resource issues facing coastal Mendocino County.

Communicate clearly when writing or speaking about ecological issues of coastal Mendocino County, demonstrating content knowledge of key ecological concepts and their social, political, and historical context.
Observe and identify the diversity of habitats within the coastal Mendocino County and their associated fauna and flora.

rows.title: Habitat Restoration Field Studies
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify the key role habitat restoration plays in species conservation, ecosystem function, and sustaining ecosystem services on which humanity relies.
Apply necessary ecological concepts needed to design a functioning habitat.
Evaluate the techniques involved in habitat restoration.

rows.title: Introduction to Genetics
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Explain genetic inheritance, variation, and regulation at the molecular level.
Apply concepts of cell division, chromosome structure, and gene interactions to solve complex genetic problems.
Evaluate the utility of various technologies used in modern genetic analysis and engineering.
Construct an argument for evolutionary theory using the basic principles of genetic variability, inheritance and population genetics.

rows.title: Practical Mathematics for Laboratory Science
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Analyze measurements of weight, volume and dimensions.
Analyze and graph algebraic equations.
Compare fractions, percentages and decimals to each other.
Carry out calculations common to a scientific laboratory setting using algebraic and statistical methods.

rows.title: Biotechnology Laboratory Techniques
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Prepare laboratory solutions and media using proper calculation methods, laboratory equipment, and techniques.
Describe basic concepts of chemistry and molecular and cell biology with respect to their role in biological systems and experimental procedures.
Perform basic laboratory techniques, including bacterial growth and transformation, DNA purification, analysis, and spectroscopy.
Maintain an accurate and organized record of lab work, results, and analysis of experiments in a laboratory notebook.
Employ laboratory safety and Good Manufacturing Practices

rows.title: Stem Cell Technology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Use industry standard techniques to maintain stem cell cultures in an undifferentiated state.
Execute standard protocols and culture techniques to induce differentiation of stem cells into different cell types.
Analyze stem cells and differentiated cells using standard techniques such as phase microscopy, immunofluorescence, and flow cytometry.
Relate cultural and social attitudes to ethical issues and governmental policies concerning stem cell research.
Apply critical thinking to interpret experiments with stem cells.

rows.title: Western Blotting Techniques
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Describe the biological and theoretical principles of Western blotting technique using industry-standard terminology.
Explain basics of monoclonal and polyclonal antibody structure, mechanism of function, and usage as it relates to Western blots.
Perform standard Western blotting procedures.
Record and analyze Western blot procedures and data in industry-standard laboratory notebooks.
Describe applications of Western blotting technique.

rows.title: Briefings in Biotechnology
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify and evaluate ethical issues associated with advances in biotechnology discovery.
Explain career and educational trajectories in the field of biotechnology and related sciences
Analyze and discuss biological concepts utilizing proper terminology.

rows.title: Engineering Detailing in Revit®
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Identify Revit platform's user interfaces
Modify 3D Revit models using the bidirectional method
Create a simple 3D residential model in a 3D CAD environment
Create 2D drawings from a Revit model
Integrate 2D CAD files, image files, and spreadsheets into Revit projects

rows.title: 3D Printing & Solid Modeling
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate the benefits and impacts of 3D printing
Create a 3D model in appropriate software designed for 3D printing
Produce a 3D printed object while making efficient use of material and resolution

rows.title: Culinary Fundamentals: Baking and Pastry
rows.heading: STUDENT LEARNING OUTCOMES
rows.lead: Upon completion of this course, a student will be able to:
